extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theology and law; Christian princes and theologians
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of criteria that distinguish ecclesiastical counsel from civil law, and of the limits of episcopal and papal jurisdiction relative to civil sovereignty in a Christian commonwealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between Law and Counsell
rubrics_metrics.description: The reason of a Law is taken from the design and benefit of him that prescribeth it; but the reason of a Counsell, from the design and benefit of him to whom the Counsell is given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use origin-of-benefit test to classify a prescription: if it aims at the prescriber's benefit (and backed by coercive power) it is a Law; if it aims at the recipient's salvation or good, it is Counsel. (Reference: chap. 25 and repeated argument.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Apostolic Acts are Counsels, not Laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The Acts of the Apostles and their Epistles are counsels because the Apostles aimed only at the benefit (salvation) of converted Gentiles and would receive reward whether obeyed or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat apostolic directives as exhortations lacking civil legislative force unless accompanied by civil sovereignty or coercive sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ecclesiastical Princes are Civil Sovereigns to have Temporal Jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no Ecclesiastical Princes except those that are also Civil Sovereigns; their principalities exceed not the compass of their civil sovereignty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that spiritual office alone (absent civil sovereignty) does not confer temporal princely authority; bishops without civil sovereignty may be doctors but not princes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excommunication is Spiritual Censure, Not Civil Punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Excommunication, without the civil power, is no more but a leaving of their company and having no more to do with them than with a Heathen man or a Publican; it is not in its own nature a punishment but a denouncing of punishment to be inflicted by Christ at Judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate ecclesiastical censures with civil punishments (death, imprisonment, fines). Such spiritual censures do not supply legislative power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biblical Metaphors of Rod and Punishment Refer to Spiritual Discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: References such as 'Shall I come unto you with a Rod, or in love...' signify spiritual discipline (excommunication / denunciation), not the magistrate's power to punish offenders by temporal means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret scriptural imagery of chastisement in pastoral/eschatological terms rather than as authorization for temporal coercion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imperative Language in Apostolic Letters does not Make Laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Commanding or imperative words in the Apostles' letters (e.g., precepts to Timothy) are wise precepts or counsel, not laws, because Timothy was a disciple, not a civil sovereign authoritatively commanding subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the speaker's office and audience: imperative tone alone is insufficient to establish civil law; legislative status requires sovereign authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hearing Pastors ≠ Legal Obligation; Obedience Grounded in Benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: To 'hear' those sent by Christ means hearken and put into practice for one's own benefit; obedience to pastors derives from concern for salvation, not from their legislative power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish moral/spiritual deference from juridical obligation; subjects may follow pastoral counsel for their souls but may still dispute doctrine (e.g., test the spirits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws Require Civil Sovereignty and Power to Punish
rubrics_metrics.description: Jurisdiction and lawmaking belong to him who has power to prescribe rules of right and wrong and to compel obedience with the sword of justice; without that civil power, decrees are not laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating whether a rule is a law, check for the presence of coercive civil authority and mechanisms to enforce punishments; absent these, the rule is counsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bishops' Jurisdiction is Derivative from Civil Sovereigns (Not Immediate De Jure Divino)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bishops have authority in a Christian commonwealth by derivation from the civil sovereign; they do not (in general) hold jurisdiction immediately from God (De Jure Divino) except in territories where the Pope is also civil sovereign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine the source of episcopal jurisdiction by reference to the local civil sovereign's grant or recognition; equality or disparity among bishops' jurisdictions indicates human, not divine, origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Papal Temporal Power Limited to Territories Where He Is Civil Sovereign
rubrics_metrics.description: The Pope is not lord of all the world nor of all Christendom; where he lacks civil sovereignty he has no direct temporal jurisdiction and cannot validly depose or transfer kingdoms except where civil power has been given or ceded to him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat papal claims to depose princes or transfer kingdoms skeptically unless there's clear civil or consensual basis; historical papal practice does not by itself establish universal temporal right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordination of Civil to Spiritual is Misconstrued if Taken to Mean Subject Persons
rubrics_metrics.description: If civil government is a means to spiritual felicity, that subordination of means does not imply the subjection of the civil sovereign to the spiritual sovereign; subordination of actions is not subjection of persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid inferring personal political subjection from teleological subordination; test claims of spiritual authority to command temporal rulers on the basis of person-to-person rights, not purpose-to-means relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: There is No Universal Earthly Christian Commonwealth with a Single Representative
rubrics_metrics.description: Christian kings, popes, clergy, and laity do not make but one commonwealth on earth; each kingdom (France, Spain, Venice, etc.) is a separate commonwealth represented by its sovereign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept arguments that assume a single earthly 'Church' commonwealth whose representative (the Pope) can exercise universal civil authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: If Authority Can Be Taken Away by a Prince, It Is Not Immediate from God
rubrics_metrics.description: If a supposed divine jurisdiction can be deprived or altered by a king (as Abiathar was deprived by Solomon), then that jurisdiction is not held immediately from God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the test: susceptibility to deprivation by temporal sovereign indicates human/derivative origin of the office or power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to Teach Does Not Entail Coercive Power Over Kings
rubrics_metrics.description: The pastoral power given (e.g., 'Feed my sheep') is a command to teach; it does not by itself grant the coercive authority to depose or command kings in temporal matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting pastoral commission, confine its practical political import to teaching and spiritual care unless explicit civil powers are also granted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical Examples Do Not Prove Legitimacy of Ecclesiastical Temporal Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples (e.g., excommunications, papal translations of empires) do not by their occurrence demonstrate rightful authority; many such acts were crimes or acts done in the pope's own cause and thus void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat precedent and historical practice as insufficient proof of rightful power; evaluate legality and origin of acts, not merely their occurrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obey God over Man when Commands Conflict and Divine Origin is Known
rubrics_metrics.description: When a man receives two contrary commands and knows that one is God's, he ought to obey God and not the lawful sovereign or father who commands otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In clear cases of divine command, prioritize obedience to God; this is a fundamental principle but hinges on the agent's certainty that the command is genuinely divine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty of Distinguishing Divine Commands from Abuses of God's Name
rubrics_metrics.description: A major source of sedition is the uncertainty whether a command given 'in the name of God' is truly from God or a misuse of God's name for private ends; subjects may not be competent to judge this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the epistemic and political danger: when people cannot reliably discern divine commands, claims of divine authority may generate civil unrest. This cautions against empowering actors to enforce 'commands of God' absent civil adjudication.
